Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 19, verse 4:

As for the words of Zakariyya, ﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾, it has been said that this is a supplication of request. The meaning is: You have accustomed me to answering and granting me what I ask, and You have not made me wretched by rejection and deprivation. So it is a means of seeking nearness to Him, the Exalted, through what preceded of His answering and His kindness, just as it is related that a man asked another man and said, "I am the one you did good to at such and such a time."

He said, "Welcome to one who seeks nearness to us through ourselves, and who has had his need fulfilled."

This is evident here, and it is indicated by the fact that he put this before his request for a child and made it a means to his Lord. So he asked Him to continue with him according to the custom He had accustomed him to, of fulfilling his needs, in what he asked.

(Section)

Al-Hasan said: "The reward of a secret supplication over a public one is seventy times. The Muslims would strive in supplication, and no sound of theirs would be heard except a whisper between them and their Lord. That is because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾. And Allah, the Exalted, mentioned a righteous servant and approved of his action, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾."

There are many benefits in concealing supplication:

The first: it is greater in faith, because its doer knows that Allah, the Exalted, hears his hidden supplication. He is not like the one who says that Allah hears if we speak aloud but does not hear if we conceal.

The second: it is greater in courtesy and reverence. For this reason kings are not addressed nor asked with raised voices; rather, voices are lowered before them and speech is kept soft to the degree that they can hear it. Whoever raises his voice before them is despised. And to Allah belongs the highest likeness. So if He hears the hidden supplication, nothing befitting courtesy before Him except lowering the voice in it.

The third: it is more effective in humility and submissiveness, which is the spirit, core and purpose of supplication. The humble, lowly, submissive one asks as a poor, abased person whose heart is broken, whose limbs are humbled and whose voice is subdued, to the point that his abasement, poverty, brokenness and submissiveness may nearly make his tongue fail, so that he does not contend with speech. His heart is a seeker, a beseecher, supplicating, while his tongue, from the intensity of his lowliness, submissiveness and poverty, is silent. With this state, raising the voice in supplication is not possible at all.

The fourth: it is more effective in sincerity.

The fifth: it is more effective in gathering the heart upon Allah, the Exalted, in supplication, for raising the voice scatters and disperses it. The lower the voice, the more effective it is in focusing and concentrating the aim and intention upon the One being called upon, glorified and exalted be He.

The sixth, and it is one of the wondrous secret subtleties: it indicates the nearness of its doer to Allah, and that because of his closeness to Him and the intensity of his presence, he asks Him a request as if he were asking the nearest thing to Him. He thus asks in the manner of intimate conversation with One who is near, not in the manner of calling a distant one from afar. For this reason, He, glorified, praised His servant Zakariyya by saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾. So whenever the heart keeps in mind the nearness of Allah, the Exalted, to it, and that He is nearer to it than any near one, and it contemplates this, it conceals its supplication as much as it can, and it does not find it fitting to raise the voice with it, but rather regards that as unbecoming. This is like someone who addresses a companion who hears his whispered speech: if he exaggerates in raising his voice, that is found distasteful from him. And to Allah belongs the highest likeness, glorified be He.

The Prophet (ﷺ) indicated this very meaning in the sound hadith, when the Companions raised their voices with the takbir while they were with him on a journey. He said:

"Be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. You are calling upon One who is All-Hearing, near, nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount."

And He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the call of the caller when he calls upon Me.﴾

(Benefit)

The secret, and God knows best, behind the caliphate passing from the People of the House of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman is this:

If Ali had assumed the caliphate after his death, the falsifiers would have been quick to say that it was a kingdom whose rule was inherited by his household. So God protected the station of His messengership and prophethood from this doubt.

Consider the words of Heraclius to Abu Sufyan: "Did any of his forefathers hold kingship?" He said: "No." Heraclius said to him: "If any of his forefathers had been a king, I would have said that he is a man seeking the kingdom of his forefathers."

So God protected his lofty station from the suspicion of kingship among his forefathers and his household.

This, and God knows best, is also the secret behind the Prophets not bequeathing their property, definitively, for this very reason: lest the falsifier think that the Prophets sought to amass worldly wealth for their children and heirs, as a person does out of attachment to himself, bequeathing his wealth to his offspring and descendants. God protected them from this and prevented them from passing any property on to their heirs, lest accusation reach the proofs of God and His messengers, so that no doubt would remain at all about their prophethood and messengership. And one should not say: "Ali and his household did in fact assume it." For the matter has already been established that it is not an inherited kingdom, but rather a caliphate of prophethood, which is earned through precedence and merit. Ali, in his time, was the foremost of the Community and its best, and there was none among them, at the time it was assumed, more entitled to it than he, nor better than him. Thus no doubt was produced for a falsifier by this. And all praise is due to God, the Exalted.

Allah the Exalted said to Maryam: ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates. So eat and drink and be content.﴾

In the Two Sahihs, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Ja'far, who said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ eating cucumber with fresh dates (ruṭab)."

In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, on the authority of Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to break his fast with fresh dates (ruṭabāt) before praying. If there were no fresh dates, then dates (tamarāt); and if there were no dates, he would take a few sips of water."

The nature of fresh dates (ruṭab) is the nature of water: hot and moist. It strengthens a cold stomach and suits it, increases sexual vigor (al-bāh), nourishes the body, suits those of cold temperament, and provides abundant nourishment.

It is among the most suitable of fruits for the people of Madinah and other lands whose fruit it is, and the most beneficial of them for the body. However, for one who is not accustomed to it, it quickly causes decay in the body and generates a blood that is not praiseworthy; excessive consumption of it causes headache and melancholy (sawda'), harms the teeth, and its corrective is sakanjabin (a vinegar-and-honey drink) and the like.

In the Prophet's ﷺ breaking of the fast upon it, or upon dates, or water, there is a very subtle arrangement. Fasting empties the stomach of food, so the liver finds nothing in it to draw in and send to the powers and organs. Sweetness is the fastest thing to reach the liver and the most beloved to it, especially if it is fresh dates, so it readily accepts it, and both it and the powers benefit from it. If fresh dates are not available, then dates for their sweetness and nourishment. If these are not available, then sips of water quench the blaze of the stomach and the heat of fasting, so that after it the stomach awakens to food and takes it with appetite.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 19, verse 31:

And the statement of the Messiah: ﴿And He has made me blessed wherever I may be﴾

Several of the early scholars (al-salaf) said: "A teacher of good wherever I may be." This is part of what is implied by the name, for the blessed (mubarak) is one who abounds in good in himself, and who conveys that good to others through teaching, empowering, advising, intending well, and striving. For this reason, a servant is blessed because Allah has blessed him and made him so. Allah, the Exalted, is the Blessed (mutabarik) because all blessing comes from Him. So His servant is blessed, and He is the One who is blessed. ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan) upon His servant, that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾

And His statement: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things competent﴾.

And he said in Jala' al-Afham:

His Book is blessed, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And this is a blessed Reminder which We have sent down﴾

And the Exalted said: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed﴾. It is more worthy to be called blessed than anything else, because of the abundance of its good, its benefits, and the many aspects of blessing in it.

Ibn al-Qayyim said, after some discussion:

As for the thirteenth question, which asks about the secret behind God saying the greeting to them with the indefinite form (*nakira*, "indefinite"), while He prescribed for His servants to greet His Messenger with the definite form (*ma'rifa*, "definite"), and likewise their greeting of themselves and of His righteous servants: the wisdom in the greeting being in the indefinite form has already been explained. Here we add another benefit. It has been mentioned before that the presence of the *alif-lam* (the definite article "al-") in *al-salam* (the greeting, "peace") has four benefits. This context does not need them, because the one who speaks the greeting is God, the Exalted. He does not intend blessing (*tabarruk*, "seeking blessing") through mentioning the Name, as the servant intends it, because seeking blessing is requesting and drawing down blessing, and it is the servant who intends that. Nor does He intend the entreaty and petition that the servant intends, nor does He intend generality. This is also not fitting here, because a greeting from Him, glorified is He, is sufficient in place of every greeting, suffices in place of every salutation, and brings near every wish. Even the least of His greetings encompasses every attribute, completes the blessing, repels misery, makes life pleasant, and cuts off the causes of ruin and destruction. So there is no meaning to mentioning the *alif-lam* there.

Reflect on His saying: ﴿God has promised the believing men and the believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence; and approval from God is greater﴾. How He brought *al-ridwan* (approval) as an indefinite subject, and reported about it that it is greater than everything they were promised. The least of His approval is greater than the gardens and the pleasant dwellings within them and all they contain. This is why, when He manifests Himself to His friends in the Gardens of Eden and asks them what they wish, they say: "Our Lord, what could we want that is better than what You have given us?" Then the Blessed and Exalted says: "Indeed I have something better than that for you: I shall make My approval descend upon you, so I shall never be displeased with you after this, ever."

It has become clear from this the difference between God's greeting upon His messengers and servants and the greeting of the servants upon them. The greeting of the servants, since it includes the benefits of the *alif-lam* mentioned earlier, namely the intention of seeking blessing through His Name *al-Salam*, the indication of asking peace for Him, requesting it from God by the Name *al-Salam*, and intending the generality of peace, it is better for the Muslim addressing the Messenger to say: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of God and His blessings." Although "Peace be upon you" (*salam 'alayka*) has been reported, the definite form is more frequent, more sound, and more complete in meaning, so one should not turn away from it, and in this context one should not be stingy with the *alif-lam*. And God knows best.

(Section)

As for the fifteenth question, which asks about the wisdom in restricting the greeting, in the stories of Yahya and the Messiah, may the prayers of God be upon them both, to these three times:

Its secret, and God knows best, is that the seeking of safety becomes more emphatic in the situations that are places of ruin and occasions of loneliness. Whenever a place is more likely to be such, the seeking of safety becomes more emphatic and aspiration attaches to it. These three situations are mentioned because safety is more emphatic in them, seeking it is more important, and the soul is more eager for it, because the servant in them has moved from a dwelling in which the soul was settled, accustomed to its companionship and residence, to another dwelling in which he is exposed to calamities, trials and afflictions. The fetus, from the moment it leaves for this dwelling, is set up to face its afflictions, its hardships, its distresses and its trials, as the poet has expressed this meaning clearly when he says:

Reflect on the crying of the infant at its emergence
into this world, when it is born.
You will find beneath it a wondrous secret, as if
it is threatened by all that it encounters.

And if not, what makes it cry from it, when it is wider than what it was in and more comfortable?

This is why, from the moment it came out, the devil's jab in its side hastened to it, so it cried because of that, and because of the loneliness that befell it through separation from its first homeland. This is what the physicians and naturalists have grasped. As for what the Messenger reported, there is nothing in their discipline that indicates it, just as there is nothing in it that negates it. So seeking safety in these situations is among the most emphatic matters.

The second situation is its departure from this dwelling to the dwelling of the *barzakh* (the intermediate realm) at death. The relation of this world to that dwelling is like the relation of its dwelling in its mother's womb to this world, as an approximation and an illustration; otherwise the matter is greater and larger than that. Seeking safety when it moves to that dwelling is also among the most important matters.

The third situation is the situation of the Day of Resurrection, the day on which God, the Exalted, raises the living, and no dwelling before it has any relation to it. Seeking safety on it is more emphatic than everything before it, for its ruin cannot be remedied, its stumble cannot be undone, its sickness cannot be cured, and its poverty cannot be filled.

So reflect on how He singled out these situations for the greeting because of the great need for safety in them. Recognize the worth of the Qur'an and what it contains of secrets, treasures of knowledge and insights, of which the minds of all creatures are unable to count a tenth. And reflect on what the greeting contains, beyond safety, of intimacy and the removal of loneliness. Then apply that to the loneliness that befalls the servant in these three situations: when he comes out into the world of trial, when he witnesses the terror of the moment of arrival when he comes before God alone and stripped of every companion except the good deeds he sent forward, and when he reaches the Resurrection together with the vast multitude, so that he may proceed to one of the two abodes for which he was created and be made to act by the deeds of its people. Which situation is more deserving of seeking safety than these situations? So we ask God for safety in them, by His bounty, generosity, kindness, munificence and benevolence.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 19, verse 39:

It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Death will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the shape of a horned ram, white with black spots (kabsh amlah). It will be stopped between Paradise and the Fire, and it will be said: 'O people of Paradise, do you recognize this?' They will crane their necks and look and say: 'Yes. This is Death.' Then it will be said: 'O people of the Fire, do you recognize this?' They will crane their necks and look and say: 'Yes. This is Death.' He said: Then it will be commanded that it be slaughtered. He said: Then it will be said: 'O people of Paradise, eternity without death; and O people of the Fire, eternity without death.'" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be decided, while they are in heedlessness and do not believe.﴾ Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh).

Also in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people of Paradise will enter Paradise and the people of the Fire will enter the Fire. Then a caller (mu'adhdhin) will stand among them and say: 'O people of Paradise, there is no death; and O people of the Fire, there is no death. Each one will abide forever in what he is in.'"

And from him (Ibn 'Umar) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise have gone to Paradise and the people of the Fire have gone to the Fire, Death will be brought until it is placed between the Fire and Paradise. Then a caller will call out: 'O people of Paradise, there is no death. O people of the Fire, there is no death.' So the people of Paradise will increase in joy, and the people of the Fire will increase in grief."

And from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, Death will be brought seized by the collar (mulabbaban), and it will be stopped at the wall (sur) that is between the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire. Then it will be said: 'O people of Paradise!' and they will look up fearfully. Then it will be said: 'O people of the Fire!' and they will look up joyfully, hoping for intercession. It will be said to the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire: 'Do you recognize this?' Both groups will say: 'We have recognized it; it is the Death that was entrusted to us.' Then it will be thrown down and slaughtered on the wall. Then it will be said: 'O people of Paradise, eternity without death; and O people of the Fire, eternity without death.'"

Narrated by al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi, and al-Tirmidhi said: hasan sahih (a sound and reliable hadith).

This ram, the throwing down, the slaughter, and the two groups witnessing that are a reality, not imagination or allegory, as some people have erred in this, a grievous error. They said: Death is an accident ('arad), and an accident does not take on a body, let alone be slaughtered.

This is not correct. Allah, glorified is He, creates from death the form of a ram that is slaughtered, just as He creates from deeds forms by which their doers are rewarded and punished. Allah, exalted is He, creates from accidents bodies of which accidents are the matter, and He creates from bodies accidents, just as He creates from accidents accidents, and from bodies bodies.

So the four categories are possible and within the power of the Lord, exalted is He, and they do not entail a combination of contradictories or anything impossible. There is no need for the strained claim of those who say that the slaughter is for the Angel of Death. All of this is corrupt presumption against Allah and His Messenger, and false interpretation that neither reason nor transmission requires. Its cause is a lack of understanding of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended by his words, so this speaker supposed that the wording of the hadith indicates that the accident itself is slaughtered.

Another mistaken person supposed that the accident is annihilated and disappears, and in its place a body is produced that is slaughtered. The two groups did not reach the view we have mentioned, that Allah, glorified is He, creates bodies from accidents and makes them the matter of those bodies, as in the Sahih, where he (ﷺ) said: "Al-Baqarah and Al-'Imran will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds (ghamamatan) – the hadith..." This is the recitation from which Allah, glorified is He, creates two clouds. Likewise his saying in another hadith: "What you mention of the majesty of Allah: His glorification, praise, and declaration of His oneness (tahlil)? They will encircle the Throne, having a humming like the humming of bees, mentioning their companion." Recorded by Ahmad.

Likewise his saying regarding the punishment of the grave and its bliss, concerning the form the buried person sees: "He will say: Who are you? He will say: I am your righteous deed, and I am your evil deed."

This is a reality, not imagination; rather, Allah, glorified is He, produces for the believer from his deed a beautiful form, and for the wicked person from his deed an ugly form.

Is the light that is divided among the believers on the Day of Resurrection anything other than their own faith? Allah, glorified is He, produces for them from it a light running before them?

This is a matter that reason comprehends, even if no text has mentioned it; and when a text does mention it, it is in agreement of reason and transmission.

Sa'id reported from Qatadah: "It has reached us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'When the believer comes out of his grave, Allah will present his deed to him in a beautiful form and with a good tidings, and he will say to him: Who are you? By Allah, I see you to be a man of truthfulness. He will say: I am your deed. So it will be for him a light and a guide to Paradise.' As for the disbeliever, when he comes out of his grave, his deed will be presented to him in an evil form and with evil tidings, and he will say: Who are you? By Allah, I see you to be a man of evil. He will say to him: I am your deed. Then he will be taken away until he is made to enter the Fire.'"

Mujahid said the same.

Ibn Jurayj said: His deed is presented to him in a beautiful form and a pleasant fragrance, accompanying his companion and giving him glad tidings of every good, and he says to him: Who are you? He says: I am your deed. So He makes for him a light before him until He makes him enter Paradise, and that is His saying: ﴿Their Lord will guide them by their faith﴾.

And the disbeliever has his deed presented to him in an evil form and a foul smell, clinging to his companion and tormenting him, until it casts him into the Fire.

Ibn al-Mubarak said: al-Mubarak ibn Fudalah narrated to us from al-Hasan that he recited this verse: ﴿Are we not to die except our first death, and we are not to be punished?﴾ He said: They knew that every bliss after which there is death is one that will be cut off, so they said: Are we not to die except our first death, and we are not to be punished? It was said: No. They said: Indeed, this is the great triumph.

Yazid al-Raqqashi used to say in his speech: The people of Paradise were secured from death, so life became pleasant for them, and they were secured from illnesses, so long abiding in the neighborhood of Allah became delightful for them. Then he would weep until his tears flowed down upon his beard.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 19, verses 41–45:

The saying of Abraham the Friend (al-Khalil) to his father: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, and does not avail you at all?﴾

He began his address by mentioning his fatherhood, which indicates respect for him, and he did not call him by his name. Then he brought the speech out in the form of a question, saying: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees, and does not avail you at all?﴾ and he did not say "Do not worship." Then he said: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you﴾. He did not say to him "you are ignorant, you have no knowledge," but turned away from this expression to a gentler expression that indicates the same meaning, so he said: ﴿there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you﴾. Then he said: ﴿So follow me, I will guide you to a straight path﴾. This is like the saying of Moses to Pharaoh: ﴿and I would guide you to your Lord﴾. Then he said: ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so that you become a companion to Satan﴾. He attributed the fear to himself rather than to his father, as the compassionate one who fears for someone he cares about does. He said "touch you" (yamassaka), mentioning the word "touch," which is gentler than other words. Then he made "punishment" indefinite, then he mentioned "the Most Merciful" and did not say "the Compeller" or "the Subduer." So what address is gentler and softer than this?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 19, verse 61:

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. It was said that it is the name of one garden among the gardens, but the correct view is that it is the name of a category of gardens, and all of them are "Gardens of Eden." God Most High says: ﴿Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants in the unseen.﴾

And God Most High says: ﴿Gardens of Eden, they will enter them; they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk.﴾

And God Most High says: ﴿And good dwellings in Gardens of Eden.﴾

The derivation (ishtiqaq) indicates that all of them are Gardens of Eden, for it comes from residing and remaining.

It is said: "'Adana bil-makan" when one resides in the place; "'adanat al-balad" when one settles in the town; and "'adanat al-ibil makan kadha" when the camels stay at such a place and do not leave it.

Al-Jawhari said: From it comes "Jannat 'Adn," meaning a residence. From it the word "al-ma'din" (mine), with a kasra on the dal, is named, because people reside in it summer and winter. Its origin (markaz) is that everything's "ma'din" is its source. And "al-'adin" is a she-camel that stays in the pasture.

(A Wonderful Benefit)

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every sect whichever of them was most insolent toward the Most Merciful.﴾ (Qur'an 19:69)

Al-Shī'ah (the sect) is a group whose members support one another, i.e., follow one another; from the same root comes al-ashyā' (the followers). The difference between al-shī'ah and al-ashyā' is that al-ashyā' are the followers, while al-shī'ah are the people who support one another, each following the other. It is mostly used in a negative sense, and perhaps it is not found in the Qur'an except in this way, as in this verse, and in His statement: ﴿Of those who divided their religion and became sects (shiya')﴾, and His statement: ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire, as was done with their like before (ashyā'ihim)﴾.

This is, and God knows best, because of what the word shī'ah contains of spreading (shiyā') and dissemination (ishā'ah), which are the opposite of harmony and unity. For this reason the word shiya' is applied only to groups of misguidance, because of their dispersion and disagreement. The meaning is: We will surely draw out from every sect the most insolent of them against God and the greatest of them in corruption, and We will cast them into the Fire. In this there is an indication that the punishment first falls upon the leaders, and then the followers come after them in it, just as they followed them in the world.

As for ﴿whichever of them (ayyuhum) was most (ashaddu)﴾, the grammarians have several opinions:

The first: the view of al-Khalīl that it is a subject (mubtada') and ashaddu is its predicate, and the verb "surely draw out" does not govern it, because it is a reported (mahkī) clause. The implied sense is: "the one of whom it is said: 'whichever of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful.'" According to this, ayy is interrogative.

The second: the view of Yūnus that it is in the nominative by way of suspension (ta'līq) of the preceding verb, as when you say "I knew that he is your brother," where the verb is suspended from acting upon the clause, as the verbs of the heart are suspended.

The third: the view of Sībawayh that ayy here is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), built on damm (vowel-ending), and what justifies its being built is the omission of the first element of its relative clause. In his view, the original sentence was "whichever of them is most insolent," and when the first element of the relative clause was omitted, it was built on damm, likening it to the adverbial terms whose complements have been omitted, such as qabla and ba'da.

For each of these opinions there are difficulties, which we will mention, and then we will show the correct view, God willing.

As for the view of al-Khalīl, it is said that it entails six matters:

The first: the omission of the antecedent (al-mawṣūf).

The second: the omission of the relative clause (al-ṣilah).

The third: the omission of the returning pronoun (al-'ā'id), since its implied form would be "the one to whom it is said that they are most insolent," and we have no precedent for this in the language.

As for what is omitted from speech, it is only a bare saying not functioning as a relative clause of a relative pronoun, as in His statement: ﴿And the angels stretch out their hands: "Bring out your souls!"﴾, meaning "saying" or "those saying." Similar is His statement: ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him, [saying]: "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to God in closeness."﴾

The fourth: that if the omitted element is estimated in this way, the sentence does not hold together, for it becomes: "We will surely draw out from every sect those of whom it is said: 'whichever of them is most insolent.'" This is invalid, for that which is drawn out is not itself described as "whichever of them is most insolent"; rather it is itself the most insolent, or one of the most insolent of the sects against the Most Merciful, so the interrogative does not fall upon it after it is drawn out. Reflect on this.

The fifth: that the interrogative occurs only after verbs of knowledge and speech in reported form, and does not occur after other verbs. You say "I knew whether Zayd is with you or 'Amr," but if you said "I struck whether Zayd or 'Amr," it would not be permitted. "Surely draw out" is not a verb of knowledge.

If you say: "I struck whichever of them stood," it can only be a relative construction, and it is not valid to say "I struck the one of whom it is said 'whichever of them stood'." Such an apparent possibility arises only because the wording is suitable for another valid sense, so someone may suppose that taking it in that other sense is correct. What shows this is that if you put in its place a clear interrogative with no other sense, it would not be permitted. So if you say, "Did Zayd strike, or 'Amr, at your place?" it is not permitted, unlike "Whichever of them struck at your place?"

If ayyuhum were an interrogative, speech would be permitted with the interrogative that has the same meaning as them, but the interrogative occurs only after verbs of knowledge and speech. As for speech, it is because every declarative or imperative clause may be reported by it. As for verbs of knowledge, the interrogative follows them because the interrogative is a request for information, so that when you say, "Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?", the meaning is "Inform me," and when you say, "I knew whether Zayd is with you or 'Amr," the meaning is "I knew what its information was sought to be." This is why the interrogative is permitted after knowledge, since it is a seeking of information; then the verbs of supposition and assumption were analogized to them, since they belong to their category, and also because of the frequent use of verbs of knowledge, which made them the customary case, unlike others.

The sixth: that this omission which is estimated in the verse is an omission not indicated by the context; it is of unknown placement, and every omission of this kind is a matter of the knowledge of the unseen. As for the view of Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb, its difficulty is evident, for suspension occurs only with verbs of the heart such as knowing, thinking and supposing, and not with others.

It is not permitted to say "I struck whichever of them stood" with ayy as an interrogative while the verb has been suspended from governing it. As for the view of Sībawayh, its difficulty is that it is a construction outside the parallels, and no evidence for it has been found in the language. Al-Suhaylī said: "What Sībawayh mentioned, if it were supported by a witness from verse or prose, or if we found after him in eloquent speech a witness for it, we would not turn away from his view or see any other view as superior to it. But we do not accept what lies between [these claims], especially since it contradicts others. We do not grant that anything was omitted from the speech, even if one says there must be an omission; the estimate would be 'whichever of them is your brother,' and then it is said: they did not build in the indefinite, so they do not say 'I passed by a man, your brother,' or 'I saw a man, your father,' meaning 'he is your brother and your father.' And why did they single out ayy in particular, among all other nouns, to have its relative clause omitted and then be built because of that omission? Whenever we find a part of the sentence omitted and then the noun described by the sentence built because of that omission, and that omission is not one we consider as containing the meaning of a particle or resembling one, this is the reason for building, and it is absent in ayy." The preferred view is the view of al-Khalīl, but it requires explanation. That is, he did not intend by "reporting" what comes to mind as the implied meaning of "saying," but he intended the reporting of the interrogative form itself, which is the basis of ayy, just as it is reported after knowledge when you say, "I knew who your brother is, and whether Zayd stood or sat." You have left the sentence in its state before the verb entered, because the meaning of specification and determination that was present in ayy remains, and it is an interrogative, because that meaning is what it was established for, whether as interrogative or declarative. Just as they reported the vocative particle in their saying, "O God, forgive me, O man (ayyuhā al-rajul)," and "have mercy upon us, O company (ayyatuhā al-'iṣābah)," we report the form of this to indicate the determination and specification present in the state of address, because the meaning of specification and determination exists in it. He said: As for Yūnus's view that the verb is suspended, it is correct even if it is not a verb of the heart, and the reason for its suspension is what we have mentioned about reporting the interrogative form for specification. When you complete the cause and say, "I struck whichever of them is your brother," the resemblance to the interrogative disappears, and the declarative meaning predominates in it because of the complete relative clause following it.

He said: As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And those who did wrong will know what kind of return they will be returned to﴾ (26:227), and the consensus that it is in the accusative governed by ﴿yanqalibūn﴾ and not by ﴿sa-ya'lamu﴾. It could have been conceived that it is governed by "sa-ya'lamu" as an interrogative, but it would be a relative clause with the clause as its relative sentence and an omitted returning pronoun. But this is prevented by a principle we established and a proof we set forth: that when the relative noun is intended as a verbal noun and connected to a verb derived from that verbal noun, it is not permitted, because the desired benefit of the relative clause, which is clarifying and explaining the relative, is absent; a verbal noun does not clarify the verb derived from its own form, since it is in a sense the same thing in wording and meaning, except in differing kinds, as previously mentioned.

He said: There is another point stronger than this, which is that ayy does not mean "the one who" unless it is annexed to a definite noun. So you say, "I met whichever of them is in the house," because it is impossible for it to mean "the one who" while it is indefinite, and "the one who" is not indefinite. This is a principle upon which the understanding of ayy is built.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 19, verses 71–72:

Ahmad narrated from him (ﷺ): "Whoever stands guard behind the Muslims in the way of Allah, voluntarily, and no ruler seizes him, he will not see the Fire with his own eyes except as the fulfilment of the oath (taḥillat al-qasam). For Allah says: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass through it.﴾"

And he (ﷺ) said to a man who guarded the Muslims during a night of their journey, from its beginning until morning, upon the back of his horse, and did not dismount except for prayer or to relieve himself: "You have earned it; there is no harm for you if you do not work after it."

(Faʾida, a benefit)

When the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "No one who pledged allegiance under the tree will enter the Fire," Ḥafṣa said to him: "Did not Allah say: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass through it﴾?"

He said: "Did you not hear His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah and leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees﴾?"

So the reconciliation of the two texts was unclear to her, and she thought that "wurūd" (coming to, passing through) meant entering it, as one says "waarada al-madīna" when one enters it. The Prophet (ﷺ) answered that the arrival (wurūd) of the righteous is not the arrival of the wrongdoers: the righteous arrive at it in a way by which they are saved from its punishment, while the wrongdoers arrive at it in a way by which they end up kneeling within it. So the arrival is not like the arrival.

(Laṭīfa, a subtle point)

When the people prepared for the Battle of Mu'ta, and they were three thousand, and the time of their departure arrived, the people bade farewell to the commanders of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and greeted them. Then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa wept, and they said: "What makes you weep?"

He said: "By Allah, it is not love of this world that I feel, nor longing for you. But I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite a verse of the Book of Allah in which He mentions the Fire: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass through it; it is a decree binding upon your Lord, already decreed﴾."

"So I do not know how I will have the return (ṣadr) after the passing through (wurūd)?"

The Muslims said: "May Allah accompany you with safety, and ward off harm from you, and return you to us righteous." ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa then said:

*Yet I ask the Most Merciful for forgiveness,*
*and a strike with a wide wound that hurls the foam,*

*Or a thrust with two hands of a Ḥarrān man, that finishes,*
*with a spear that pierces the entrails and the liver,*

*So that when they pass by my grave they say:*
*"May Allah guide you, O one who fought and was rightly guided."*

[Section: The third of the corruptors of the heart: attachment to other than Allah, may He be blessed and exalted]

This is the greatest of its corruptors absolutely.

There is nothing more harmful to him than this, nor anything that cuts him off more from his welfare and happiness. For when he attaches himself to other than Allah, Allah leaves him to that to which he has attached himself, and forsakes him from the direction of what he has attached himself to. He fails to attain what he seeks from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by his attachment to another and his turning toward someone other than Him. So he gains neither his portion from Allah, nor does he reach what he hoped for from the one to whom he attached himself. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah that they might be for them a source of might. No! They will deny their worship of them and will become opponents to them﴾.

And He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, hoping they might be helped. They cannot help them, and they are a force brought forward for them﴾ [Ya-Sin: 74-75].

So the most forsaken of people is the one who attaches himself to other than Allah, for what he has lost of his welfare, happiness and success is greater than what he has gained from the one to whom he attached himself, and that (gain) is exposed to ending and loss. The likeness of one who attaches himself to other than Allah is that of one who seeks shade from heat and cold beneath a spider's web, the weakest of houses.

In sum, the foundation and base of polytheism, upon which attachment to other than Allah is built, brings its bearer blame and forsaking, as Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken﴾ [al-Isra: 22]. Reproached, with no one to praise you; forsaken, with no one to help you. For some people may be overpowered yet praised, like one who was overcome by falsehood; some may be blamed yet victorious, like one who was overcome and subjugated by falsehood; and some may be praised and victorious, like one who gained power and dominion through truth. The polytheist who attaches himself to other than Allah falls into the worst of the four categories: neither praised nor victorious.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 19, verse 83:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "taghriyuhum igharaʾ" (they incite them with incitement). In another report: "tushlihim ishlaʾan" (they urge them with urging).

In another wording: "tuhrithuhum tahrīḍan" (they stir them up with stirring up). In another: "tuzʿijuhum ilā al-maʿāṣī izʿājan" (they drive them to sins with driving). In another: "tuwaqqiduhum" (they kindle them).

That is, they move them as water is moved by a fire kindled beneath it. Al-Akhfash said: "tuwahhijuhum" (they make them blaze).

The reality of this is that "al-azz" is moving and agitating. From it comes the word "al-azīz" for the bubbling of a cooking pot, because the water moves when it boils. From the hadith: "In his chest there is an azīz like the azīz of a cauldron, from weeping."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "al-azīz" is flaring up and movement, like the blaze of fire in firewood. It is said: "izz qidrak," meaning, kindle the fire beneath it. And "ayyazat al-qidr" means when its boiling intensified. So the word azz has two meanings: one is moving, and the other is kindling and inflaming. These two are close, for it is a specific movement accompanied by driving and inflaming.

This is the authority (sultan) that they have over their allies and the people of shirk. But they have no authority of proof or evidence over them. They only responded to him by his mere calling them, because it agreed with their desires and aims. Thus they are the ones who helped against themselves and enabled their enemy to have authority over them, by agreeing with him and following him. When they gave themselves over and submitted to him, he was empowered over them as a punishment for them. By this the meaning of His saying, glory be to Him, becomes clear: ﴿And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers﴾ [al-Nisa: 141].

(Section)

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾

That is, they drive them to sins with driving. Whenever they slacken or weaken, the devils drive them, stir them and incite them. They do not cease to lead the servant to sin, and to organize the gathering of their company with the subtlest trick and the most complete scheme. He has been content for himself to be the pimp for the immoral sons of Adam. He is the one who was arrogant and refused to prostrate to their father with that pride and haughtiness, yet he does not accept for himself to become the procurer for everyone who disobeys Allah, as one of them said:

"I am amazed at Iblis in his bewilderment,
and at the ugliness of the arrogance he displayed.
He was proud before Adam in a prostration...
and became a procurer for his offspring."

So the root of every sin and affliction is only whispering (waswasa). For this reason He described him with it, so that seeking refuge from its evil would be more important than from anything else one seeks refuge from. Otherwise, his evil beyond whispering is also present. Among his evils is that he is a thief who steals people's wealth. So every food or drink over which the name of Allah, the Exalted, is not mentioned, he has a share in it by theft and snatching. Likewise, he spends the night in a house when the name of Allah is not mentioned in it, so he eats the food of humans without their permission and sleeps in their houses without their command. He enters as a thief and leaves as a raider, and points out their weaknesses. He commands the servant to disobedience, then casts into people's hearts, awake and in dreams, that he did such and such. Among this is that a servant commits a sin that no one among the people sees, then in the morning people are talking about it. This is only because Satan adorned it for him and cast it into his heart, then whispered to people about what he did and cast it. He made him fall into the sin and then exposed him by it. The Lord, the Exalted, covers him, and Satan strives to uncover his cover and expose him. So the servant is deceived and says, "This is a sin that no one saw except Allah, the Exalted," and he does not realize that his enemy is striving to spread it and expose him. Few people notice this subtle point.

Among his evils is that when the servant sleeps, he ties a knot on his head that prevents him from waking, as in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Satan ties three knots on the nape of the head of one of you when he sleeps, striking upon each knot: 'For you is a long night, so sleep.' If he wakes and remembers Allah, one knot is undone. If he performs ablution, another knot is undone. If he prays, all the knots are undone, and he becomes energetic and good of soul in the morning. Otherwise he becomes evil of soul and lazy." Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Among his evils is that he urinates in the ear of the servant until he sleeps till morning, as established from the Prophet ﷺ, that a man who slept the whole night until morning was mentioned before him, and he said: "That is a man in whose ears Satan urinated," or he said, "in his ears." Narrated by al-Bukhari, narrated by al-Bukhari.

Among his evils is that he sits in wait for the children of Adam on all the paths of goodness. There is no path of the paths of goodness except that Satan lies in ambush on it, striving with all his effort to prevent him from taking it. If he disobeys him and takes it, he hinders him in it, obstructs him and confuses him with objections and obstacles. If he completes his deed and finishes it, he assigns to him what nullifies its effect and turns him back on his heels.

It is enough of his evil that he swore by Allah that he would surely sit in wait for the children of Adam on His straight path, and swore that he would come to them from before them, from behind them, from their right and from their left. His evil has reached the point that he devised the scheme and exerted the trick until he expelled Adam from Paradise. Then that did not suffice him, until he sought from his offspring a share of the Fire from every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine. Then that did not suffice him, until he worked the trick to nullify the call of Allah from the earth, and aimed that the call be to himself and that he be worshipped besides Allah. So he strives with his utmost effort to extinguish the light of Allah, nullify His call, establish the call to disbelief and shirk, and erase tawhid and its signs from the earth. It is enough of his evil that he confronted Ibrahim, the Friend of the Most Merciful, until his people threw him with the catapult into the fire, but Allah repelled his plot and made the fire coolness and safety for His friend. He confronted until the Jews wanted to kill and crucify him, but Allah repelled his plot, protected the Messiah and raised him to Himself. He confronted Zakariyya and Yahya until they were killed. He incited Pharaoh until he made the great corruption on earth attractive to him, and his claim that he was their Lord Most High. He confronted the Prophet ﷺ and backed the disbelievers in killing him with all his effort, while Allah humiliated him and returned him disappointed. He sneaked toward the Prophet ﷺ with a flaming meteor, wanting to strike him with it while he was in prayer, so the Prophet ﷺ began to say, "I curse you with the curse of Allah." He helped the Jews in their sorcery against the Prophet ﷺ. If this is his condition and his aspiration in evil, then how is deliverance from him possible except by the help of Allah, His support and His protection?

(Section)

Among this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾

So the sending here is a cosmic, decreed sending, like the sending of winds, and not a religious, legislative sending. It is a sending of empowerment, unlike His saying concerning the believers: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾. This authority negated over the believers is the very thing with which He sent His soldiers against the disbelievers.

Abu Ishaq said: "The meaning of sending here is empowerment. You say, 'I have sent so-and-so upon so-and-so' when you empower him over him, as He said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the deviators﴾." So he informed that whoever follows him is empowered over him.

I say: His saying, the Exalted, supports this: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him﴾, and His saying: ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾. The word azz in the language means moving and agitating, and from it is said azīz for the boiling of the pot, because the water moves when it boils. In the hadith: "The chest of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had an azīz like the azīz of a cauldron from weeping."

The expressions of the early scholars revolve around this meaning. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "taghriyuhum igharaʾ" (they incite them with incitement).

In another report from him: "tasilluhum salla" (they stir them with stirring).

In another report: "tuhrithuhum tahrīḍan" (they stir them up with stirring up).

In another: "tuzʿijuhum lil-maʿāṣī izʿājan" (they drive them to sins with driving), and in another: "tuwaqqiduhum iqādan" (they kindle them with kindling).

That is, as water moves by the fire beneath it. Abu ʿUbayda said: "al-azīz is inflaming and movement, like the blazing of fire in firewood. It is said: 'izz qidrak,' meaning kindle the fire beneath it, and 'ittazzat al-qidr' when its boiling intensified." This is the choice of al-Akhfash. The verification is that the word combines both meanings together.

The Qadariyya said: "The meaning of 'We sent the devils upon the disbelievers' is that We left them between them and the devils; it does not mean empowerment." Abu ʿAli said: "Irsal is used in the sense of leaving between the sender and what he wants."

So the meaning of the verse is: We left the devils between them and the disbelievers, and did not prevent them from them, and did not guard them, unlike the believers concerning whom it was said: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾.

Al-Wahidi said: "The Qadariyya go to this aspect in the meaning of the verse." He said: "The meaning is not as they have gone to." Abu Ishaq said: "The preferred view is that they were sent upon them and were assigned to them because of their disbelief, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We assign to him a devil, and he is his companion﴾, and He said: ﴿And We assigned for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them﴾. The meaning of sending is only empowerment."

I say: This is what is understood from the meaning of sending, as in the hadith: "If you send your trained dog," that is, you empower it. If he leaves it between him and the game without sending it, its game is not lawful. Likewise His saying: ﴿And in ʿĀd, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾, meaning We empowered it and subjected it against them. Likewise His saying: ﴿And He sent upon them birds in flocks﴾, and likewise His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them one cry﴾. Leaving between the sender and what he is sent upon is among the requirements of this meaning, and empowerment is not complete without it. When a thing whose nature and character is to do an action is sent and you do not prevent it from doing it, this is empowerment.

Then the Qadariyya contradicted themselves in this statement. If they permit that He could prevent them from them, protect them and bring them back, they have then abandoned their own principle, for preventing the chooser from his voluntary act while his intention is sound and his inclination correct indicates that his act and his abstention are subject to the Lord's power, and this is exactly the view of the People of the Sunna. And if they say He cannot prevent them, protect them from them or bring them back, then they have made their power and will subject to an act over which the Lord has no power to prevent, and this is the most false falsehood.

Then the Qadariyya said: ﴿inciting them with incitement﴾ means commanding them to sins by commanding. They related this from al-Dahhak.

This is not to be heeded, for one does not say of someone who commands another to something that he has incited him, and the language does not support that. Even if it were correct, it would also incite the believers, for He commands them to sins more than He commands the disbelievers, since the disbeliever is quick to obey and accept from Satan, so he does not need as much command as the believer does. He commands the disbeliever once and commands the believer many times. So if azz meant commanding, it would not be specific to the disbelievers.

(Section break)

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Muhammad ibn Abbad ibn Musa al-Ukli narrated to us that he heard al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim narrating, from al-Harith, from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this verse: ﴿On the Day when We shall gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a deputation﴾ [Maryam 19:85]. He said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, is not the wafd (deputation) only a riding party?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, when they come out of their graves they will be met with white she-camels that have wings, upon which are saddles of gold, and the straps of their sandals are a light that shines, each step of which reaches as far as the eye can see. They will arrive at the gate of Paradise, from whose root two springs gush forth. When they drink from one of them, the radiance of bliss flows into their faces, and when they perform ablution with the other, their hair will never become disheveled, ever. Then they will strike the ring to open it. If you were to hear the sound of the ring, O Ali, it would reach every houri that her husband has come, and haste will overcome her, so she will send her keeper to open the door for him. Were it not that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had made him know Himself, he would fall prostrate from what he sees of the light and splendour. And [the keeper] will say: 'I am your keeper, who has been entrusted with your affair.' So he will follow him, retracing his steps, and come to his wife, and haste will overcome her, so she will come out of the tent and embrace him, and say: 'You are my beloved, and I am your beloved. I am the one who is content, so I will never be angry; I am the one who is blessed, so I will never be miserable; I am the one who abides, so I will never depart.' He will enter a house whose length from its foundation to its roof is one hundred thousand cubits, built upon pearls and rubies, with paths of red, paths of green, and paths of yellow, no path of which resembles its companion. He will come to the couch, and on it is a bed, and on the bed are seventy cushions, and on them are seventy wives, and upon each wife are seventy garments; the marrow of her shin is visible through the garments. He will have intercourse with them in the span of a single night. Beneath them flow rivers, flowing continuously: rivers of water that has not turned putrid, pure and clear with no turbidity; rivers of honey, clarified, that has not come out of the bellies of bees; rivers of wine, a delight for drinkers, which men have not pressed with their feet; and rivers of milk whose taste has not changed, which has not come out of the bellies of livestock.

When they desire food, white birds will come to them, raising their wings, and they will eat from their sides whatever colours they wish; then they fly away and depart. There are fruits hanging low, and when they desire them the branch bends down to them, and they eat whatever fruits they wish, whether standing or reclining. This is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens will be near at hand﴾ [al-Rahman 55:54]. And before them are servants like scattered pearls."

(This is a gharib hadith; its isnad is weak, and its attribution to the Prophet (ﷺ) is questionable; what is well known is that it is mawquf upon Ali.)

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Muhammad ibn Umar ibn Sulayman narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq, from al-Nu'man ibn Sa'd, concerning this verse ﴿On the Day when We shall gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a deputation﴾:

He said: "By Allah, the deputation will not be gathered on their feet; rather, they will come upon camels such as the creation has never seen, with saddles of gold and reins of chrysolite, and they will ride them until they strike the gate of Paradise."

Consider how this meaning is unveiled and made fully clear by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And every one of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾. Note how (ātīhi) is used in the singular when the intended point is to indicate that, although they all come to Him, each one of them is separate from every group, whether companion, relative, or associate. Rather, each one stands alone, so it is as if he came to Him by himself, even if he comes together with others, because his following of others has ceased and he is solely concerned with his own affair. This, in my view, is better than the distinction made by means of the (iḍāfah, grammatical annexation) and its severance, and the distinction by this means was made by al-Suhaylī, may Allah have mercy on him. So consider both distinctions.

Love and mutual affection come only through faith and righteous deeds, as the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾.

That is, He casts love between them, so some of them love others, and they show mercy and compassion to one another through the love that God has placed in some of their hearts for others.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He loves them and makes them beloved to His servants."

Harim ibn Hayyan said: "No servant turns his heart toward God, the Mighty and Majestic, except that God turns the hearts of the believers toward him, until He grants him their affection and mercy."

As for the people of disobedience and sinfulness, although there may be some kind of affection and mutual love among them, it turns into enmity and hatred, and generally this happens to them in this world before the Hereafter. In the Hereafter, however, ﴿close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾.

The leader of the monotheists (Ibrahim) said to his people: ﴿You have taken only idols instead of God out of affection among yourselves in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disbelieve in others and curse one another﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25].

(Section)

In the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"When Allah loves a servant, He calls Jibril: 'Indeed Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.' So the inhabitants of the heavens love him. Then acceptance is placed for him on the earth." In another wording in Muslim: "When Allah loves a servant, He calls Jibril and says, 'I love so-and-so, so love him.' He said: So Jibril loves him, then he calls out in the heaven, 'Indeed Allah loves so-and-so, so love him,' and the inhabitants of heaven love him. He said: Then acceptance is placed for him on the earth. And when He hates a servant, He calls Jibril and says, 'I hate so-and-so, so hate him.' He said: So Jibril hates him, then he calls out in the heaven, 'Indeed Allah hates so-and-so, so hate him,' then hatred is placed for him on the earth."

In another wording in Muslim from Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, who said: We were at 'Arafah, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz passed by while he was in charge of the pilgrimage, and the people stood up looking at him. I said to my father: "O father, I see that Allah loves 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz." He said: "What is that?" I said: "Because of the love he has in the hearts of the people." He said: "I heard Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and then he mentioned the hadith. It was also recorded by al-Tirmidhi, who added at its end: "That is the saying of Allah, the Most High: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾." End of quotation.

Some of the early scholars said in its explanation: He loves them and makes them beloved to His servants.

In the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Hour, and he said: "What have you prepared for it?" He said: "Nothing, except that I love Allah and His Messenger." He said: "You are with those whom you love."

Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "We were never happier about anything than the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'You are with those whom you love.'" Anas said: "I love the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and 'Umar, and I hope to be with them by my love for them, even if I do not do their deeds."

In al-Tirmidhi, from him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A person is with whom he loves, and he has what he has earned."

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from him, he said: "I saw the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) rejoice at something; I had not seen them rejoice at anything more intense than that. A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, a man loves a man for a good deed he does, but does not do the like of it?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'A person is with whom he loves.'" This love for Allah necessarily entails love for the sake of Allah with certainty, for among the requirements of loving the Beloved is loving what is dear to Him and hating what He hates.

Muslim recorded in his Sahih, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, the Most High, will say on the Day of Resurrection: 'Where are those who love one another for My majesty? Today I shade them in My shade, a day when there is no shade but Mine.'"

In the Jami' of Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: 'Those who love one another for My majesty will have pulpits of light; the prophets and the martyrs will envy them.'"

In another wording by someone else: "Those who love one another for the majesty of Allah will be on the Day of Resurrection upon pulpits of light; the people of the gathering will envy them."

In the Muwatta', from the hadith of Abu Idris al-Khawlani, who said: I entered the mosque of Damascus and there was a young man with bright front teeth, and the people were around him. Whenever they disagreed about something, they referred it to him and acted upon his opinion. I asked about him, and they said: "This is Mu'adh ibn Jabal." The next day I hastened to him, but found that he had preceded me to the early noon prayer, and I found him praying. I waited until he finished his prayer, then I came to him from in front of him, greeted him, and said: "By Allah, I love you for the sake of Allah." He said: "By Allah?" I said: "By Allah." He said: "By Allah?" I said: "By Allah." He then seized the edge of my cloak, pulled me to him, and said: "Rejoice, for I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Allah, blessed and exalted, said: My love is due to those who love one another for My sake, those who sit together for My sake, those who visit one another for My sake, and those who give generously for My sake.'"

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from the hadith of Abu Dhar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of deeds is love for the sake of Allah and hatred for the sake of Allah." Also in it, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the servants of Allah are people who are neither prophets nor martyrs, whom the prophets and martyrs will envy on the Day of Resurrection because of their station with Allah." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell us who they are." He said: "They are a people who love one another by the spirit of Allah, without family ties between them or wealth they exchange. By Allah, their faces are light, and they are upon light. They do not fear when people fear, and they do not grieve when people grieve." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Unquestionably, the friends of Allah - no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾.

In another wording by someone else: "Indeed, Allah has servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, whom the prophets envy because of their station with Allah." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, describe them for us, make them known to us, that we may love them." He said: "They are a people who love one another by the spirit of Allah, without wealth they exchange or family ties they maintain. They are light, their faces are light, and they are upon chairs of light. They do not fear when people fear, and they do not grieve when people grieve." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Unquestionably, the friends of Allah - no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man visited a brother of his in another village, so Allah sent an angel to wait on his path. When he came upon him, the angel said: 'Where are you going?' He said: 'I want a brother of mine in this village.' He said: 'Do you have any favor from him that you are repaying?' He said: 'No, only that I love him for the sake of Allah, the Exalted.' He said: 'I am the messenger of Allah to you: Allah has loved you as you have loved him for His sake.'"

It is sufficient, as an immediate reward for turning toward Allah, the Most High, that Allah, glorified and exalted, turns the hearts of His servants toward whoever turns toward Him, just as He turns their hearts away from whoever turns away from Him. The hearts of the servants are in the hand of Allah, not in their own hands.

(Exhortation)

How long will you keep going back and forth in pursuit of desire and of bankruptcy, and how long will you keep striving in the company of Iblis? How much tinsel is there in your deeds, and how much deception!

Where are your peers? Do you hear any faint sound from them?

Are you aware that their regret has grown intense and their sorrow great over having preferred the base? By God, they wished that they had divorced this world before the touch.

The eye of death closes, not with lowered lids, and the gaze of the one it seeks has been drowsy since it was.

Ignorance took hold of him from the moment of his birth, so the speech cried out while the mind of the man was intoxicated.
